title: What is Unity Catalog — Databricks' unified governance layer providing centralized access control (ACLs), auditing, data lineage, and data discovery across workspaces and clouds?

s1_definition.profdef: Unity Catalog is Databricks' centralized governance layer that manages access control, auditing, data lineage, and data discovery for all data and AI assets across multiple workspaces and clouds from one place. It introduces a three-level namespace of catalog, schema, and table, and lets administrators grant and revoke permissions using standard SQL grants, while automatically recording who accessed what and how data flows from source to consumer.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has many branches (workspaces), and before, each branch kept its own separate list of who could open which safe, with no shared log and no map of where money moved. It was chaos: a person fired at head office might still have keys at a branch, and nobody could trace where a suspicious transaction's data came from. Unity Catalog is like installing one central security office for the entire bank that controls every safe's keys, keeps one tamper-proof log of every door opened, draws a live map of how documents flow from one department to another, and provides a single searchable directory so staff can find the right record. One place to grant access, one place to audit, one map of data movement.
s1_definition.oneliner: Unity Catalog is Databricks' single, centralized governance layer for access control, auditing, lineage, and discovery across all workspaces and clouds, organized as catalog, schema, and table.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Unity Catalog is Databricks' centralized governance layer that manages access control, auditing, data lineage, and data discovery for all data and AI assets across multiple workspaces and clouds from one place. It introduces a three-level namespace of catalog, schema, and table, and lets administrators grant and revoke permissions using standard SQL grants, while automatically recording who accessed what and how data flows from source to consumer.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India has many branches (workspaces), and before, each branch kept its own separate list of who could open which safe, with no shared log and no map of where money moved. It was chaos: a person fired at head office might still have keys at a branch, and nobody could trace where a suspicious transaction's data came from. Unity Catalog is like installing one central security office for the entire bank that controls every safe's keys, keeps one tamper-proof log of every door opened, draws a live map of how documents flow from one department to another, and provides a single searchable directory so staff can find the right record. One place to grant access, one place to audit, one map of data movement.

**One line to remember:** Unity Catalog is Databricks' single, centralized governance layer for access control, auditing, lineage, and discovery across all workspaces and clouds, organized as catalog, schema, and table.

sections.s2_technical:
Before Unity Catalog, governance in Databricks was per-workspace: each workspace had its own metastore and its own access controls, so a company with several workspaces had to duplicate and reconcile permissions everywhere, there was no unified audit, and tracing data lineage across workspaces was impossible. Unity Catalog solves this by introducing an account-level metastore that sits above all workspaces, so you define data assets and permissions once and they apply consistently everywhere. It organizes everything in a three-level namespace, so a table is addressed as `catalog.schema.table`, for example `banking_prod.trades.settlements`, where a catalog is the top grouping, a schema, also called a database, groups tables, and the table holds the data. This replaces the old two-level `database.table` and lets you separate environments like production and development as different catalogs under one governance umbrella.

Access control is centralized and uses familiar SQL grant and revoke statements on these objects, for example `GRANT SELECT ON TABLE banking_prod.trades.settlements TO risk_analysts`. Permissions are defined on users and groups, which are managed at the account level and synchronized from the company identity provider, so when someone leaves the bank and is removed from the identity provider, their access disappears everywhere at once. Unity Catalog supports fine-grained controls including row filters and column masks, so you can, for example, let a group see trades but mask the customer account number, which matters enormously for sensitive banking data. It governs not just tables but also views, external locations in cloud storage, functions, and machine-learning models and features, giving one consistent permission model across data and AI assets.

Beyond permissions, Unity Catalog provides auditing, lineage, and discovery. Auditing automatically records access events, so you have a central, queryable log of who read or changed which asset and when, which is essential for regulatory compliance. Lineage is captured automatically at the column level as queries run, so you can see that a gold reporting table was built from specific silver tables, which were built from specific bronze ingestion tables, and you can trace a single column back to its sources or forward to every dashboard that consumes it, which is invaluable for impact analysis and audits. Discovery provides a searchable catalog with descriptions, tags, and ownership so analysts can find trustworthy data rather than guessing. A senior-level nuance is that Unity Catalog operates across clouds, so one governance model can span AWS, Azure, and GCP workspaces, and it integrates with Delta Sharing to share data securely with external parties without copying it. Another nuance for a bank is that the combination of centralized access control, automatic audit logs, column-level lineage, and masking is precisely what regulators demand, which is a major reason regulated industries adopt it, and the practical rule is to define sensitive data permissions and masks once in Unity Catalog rather than scattering them across workspaces and risking inconsistency.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, data was spread across several Databricks workspaces, each with its own access list. When a contractor's engagement ended, head office removed them from one workspace but forgot another, and the contractor retained access to sensitive trade data. There was also no single log of who had read the customer account numbers, which the auditors demanded. This is exactly the problem Unity Catalog solves: governance must be centralized so access is granted and revoked in one place and every access is logged centrally.

This is exactly how Unity Catalog works. One account-level metastore holds the three-level catalog, schema, table namespace, permissions are granted to groups synced from the identity provider so removal is global, and access events are audited automatically.

Problem 2 — The risk analysts needed to see trades to do their work, but they must not see raw customer account numbers, and the auditors needed to trace how the fraud-reporting table was derived. This calls for column masking on the sensitive column and automatic column-level lineage from the source tables to the report. These are core Unity Catalog capabilities.

Because we cannot run a real Unity Catalog, this runnable demo models its essentials. A `Metastore` holds a three-level namespace and group-based grants. An `AccessController` checks grants and applies column masks and row filters. An `AuditLog` records every access centrally. A `LineageGraph` records how tables are derived and lets you trace upstream and downstream. The demo grants a group select with a masked account column, shows an authorized masked read, a revoked user denied, a central audit query, and a lineage trace from a gold report back to its bronze sources.

Configuration file:

```yaml
# application.yml
unity-catalog:
  account-level-metastore: true
  identity-provider-sync: true
  default-catalog: banking_prod
  audit:
    enabled: true
  masking:
    account_number: true
```

```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the demo
java -cp target/unity-catalog-sim-1.0.0.jar com.bank.uc.UnityCatalogDemo

# Real Unity Catalog SQL:

#   ALTER TABLE banking_prod.trades.settlements ALTER COLUMN account_number SET MASK mask_acct;
#   SELECT * FROM system.access.audit WHERE ...;        -- central audit
#   -- lineage is captured automatically and viewed in the Catalog Explorer
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a trades settlements table addressed by the three-level name, two users synced into a risk analysts group, and a gold fraud report derived through silver and bronze layers.

Step 1: Identity sync adds Priya and a contractor to the risk analysts group, representing users coming from the company identity provider. A single central grant gives the risk analysts group select permission on the settlements table.

Step 2: Priya reads a row. The access controller checks her group grants, finds the select permission, records an allowed entry in the central audit log, and returns the row but with the account number masked to show only the last four digits, because masking is enabled on that sensitive column.

Step 3: The contractor's engagement ends and he is removed from the identity provider. Because permissions are tied to group membership synced from the provider, removing him revokes his access everywhere at once, not just in one workspace.

Step 4: The contractor then tries to read a row. The controller checks his groups, finds none because he was removed, records a denied entry in the audit log, and returns nothing, demonstrating global revocation.

Step 5: An auditor queries the central audit log for the settlements table and gets back both events, Priya's allowed read and the contractor's denied attempt, from one queryable place.

Step 6: Lineage is recorded as the pipeline builds the bronze, silver, and gold tables. Tracing upstream from the gold fraud report returns the silver clean table, then the bronze raw table, then the original Kafka event source, so an auditor can see exactly how the report was derived.

Final output:

```
Oct 30, 2026 8:28:14 AM com.bank.uc.Metastore grant
INFO: GRANT SELECT ON banking_prod.trades.settlements TO risk_analysts
INFO: priya_analyst read banking_prod.trades.settlements: account=****0789 amount=50000
WARNING: Identity sync: contractor_bob removed from IdP → access revoked across ALL workspaces
WARNING: ACCESS DENIED: contractor_bob cannot SELECT banking_prod.trades.settlements
INFO: AUDIT for banking_prod.trades.settlements: [priya_analyst SELECT ... → ALLOWED, contractor_bob SELECT ... → DENIED]
INFO: Lineage: banking_prod.reports.fraud_gold derived from [banking_prod.trades.silver_clean]
INFO: Upstream of fraud_gold: [banking_prod.trades.silver_clean, banking_prod.trades.bronze_raw, kafka.trade_events]
```

```
  │ - userGroups  │        │ + readRow()           │
  │ + grant()     │        │ - mask()              │
  │ + userHas()   │        └─────────┬────────────┘
  │ + removeUser()│                  │ records
  └──────────────┘                  ▼
                           ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐
                           │ AuditLog      │   │ LineageGraph │
                           │ + record()    │   │ + record...()│
                           │ + query()     │   │ + traceUpstream│
                           └──────────────┘   └──────────────┘

  Contract for readRow:
    Pre:  user + fully-qualified table
    Post: ALLOWED only if a group grant exists; sensitive cols masked
    Side-effect: an audit entry is always recorded (allowed or denied)

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. Metastore.grant(SELECT, settlements, risk_analysts)
  2. readRow(priya) → userHas ✓ → audit ALLOWED → account masked
  3. Metastore.removeUser(contractor)
  4. readRow(contractor) → userHas ✗ → audit DENIED
  5. AuditLog.query(settlements) → [ALLOWED, DENIED]
  6. LineageGraph.traceUpstream(fraud_gold) → silver, bronze, kafka
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Unity Catalog is Databricks' centralized governance layer, and the single sentence I give is that it provides one place to manage access control, auditing, data lineage, and data discovery for all data and AI assets across multiple workspaces and clouds. Before it, governance was per-workspace, so a company with several workspaces had to duplicate and reconcile permissions everywhere, there was no unified audit, and tracing lineage across workspaces was impossible. Unity Catalog fixes this with an account-level metastore that sits above all workspaces, and it organizes everything in a three-level namespace of catalog, schema, and table, so a table is addressed like catalog dot schema dot table, which lets you cleanly separate environments like production and development under one governance umbrella.

Access control uses familiar SQL grant and revoke statements on these objects, and permissions are given to users and groups that are synced from the company identity provider, so when someone leaves the organization and is removed from the provider, their access disappears everywhere at once rather than lingering in a forgotten workspace. It also supports fine-grained controls like column masks and row filters, so you can let a group see trades but mask the customer account number, which is exactly the kind of control a bank needs. On top of permissions it gives you three more things: automatic auditing, so there is a central queryable log of who read or changed each asset and when; automatic column-level lineage, so you can trace a gold reporting table back through the silver and bronze layers to its original source or forward to every dashboard that consumes it; and discovery, a searchable catalog with descriptions and ownership so analysts find trustworthy data.

At the National Bank of India this directly solved two painful problems. Our data was spread across several workspaces each with its own access list, and once a contractor's engagement ended we removed him from one workspace but missed another, leaving him with access to sensitive trade data, and separately the auditors wanted a single log of who had read customer account numbers. Unity Catalog centralized all of that: grants went to groups synced from the identity provider so removing the contractor revoked his access globally, every read and write was captured in one central audit log, and we applied a column mask so risk analysts could see trades but only the last four digits of the account number. When the auditors asked how the fraud reporting table was built, the automatic column-level lineage traced it straight back through silver and bronze to the original Kafka events. That combination of central access control, audit, lineage, and masking is precisely why a regulated bank adopts Unity Catalog, and the rule I follow is to define sensitive-data permissions and masks once in Unity Catalog rather than scattering them across workspaces where they drift out of sync.
